ideas.title: The Shared Document Has a Metal Cable
ideas.era: Late medieval Europe; Nuremberg printing, 1488; Cheb library context
ideas.premise: What if today the shared office reference book could be read at the table but physically could not be taken to your desk, like a chained library book?
ideas.benchmark_query: The Shared Document Has a Metal Cable history

rationale.curiosity: A literal restriction on moving a document reveals a real preservation and security practice.
rationale.cast_comedy: The cast can escalate an attempt to share one book while Mia points out that it is readable, not forbidden.
rationale.modern_contrast: Digital copy permissions become a clearly labeled analogy to a physical tether.
rationale.primary_sources: The Czech national library supplies a dated volume and explains chaining; the original fastening and broader access rules need inspection.

cast_gags.crow: Raven calls this an imaginary office sharing policy with unusually tangible limits.
cast_gags.pip: Pip pulls up his chair when the book refuses to follow him.
cast_gags.mia: Mia reminds everyone that the point is to let readers study while keeping the book in place.
cast_gags.rex: Rex declares remote access solved by moving his desk beside the reading table.
cast_gags.timmy: Timmy brings a second chair and quietly creates the first useful collaboration.

sources.institution: National Library of the Czech Republic via Google Arts & Culture
sources.locator: Summa casuum conscientiae; 1488; printed in Nurnberg; chained books description and Cheb Franciscan library context
sources.verification_scope: Official source and stated anchors, not automatic semantic entailment

ideas.fact_boundary: The institution describes chaining as a safeguard allowing study or copying, not as a ban on reading. Office software comparisons are fiction. Do not claim every medieval library used chains, that all users had unrestricted access, or that all surviving volumes retain their original chains.
research_questions: [VERIFICAR] Confirm this copy's shelfmark, provenance and surviving attachment hardware before asserting details about its particular chain or reader admission.

ideas.title: Your Promotion Comes With Platform Shoes
ideas.premise: What if today the meeting status symbol was a pair of raised Venetian chopines instead of a job title?
ideas.benchmark_query: Your Promotion Comes With Platform Shoes history

rationale.curiosity: A visible status symbol makes the historical object and joke clear in the opening beat.
rationale.cast_comedy: Pip, Mia and Rex can expose the fictional assumption that height equals authority.
rationale.modern_contrast: A dress-code status signal translates readily to a modern meeting without inventing a historic law.
rationale.primary_sources: Victoria and Albert Museum supplies a particular Venetian pair, dimensions and date range; no universal height rule follows.

cast_gags.crow: Raven opens the file on a literal but entirely fictional promotion ladder.
cast_gags.pip: Pip discovers that his borrowed status shoes do not improve his argument.
cast_gags.mia: Mia lowers the meeting podium so evidence remains visible to everyone.
cast_gags.rex: Rex makes a taller name card to compete with the footwear.
cast_gags.timmy: Timmy places the tiny badge at table height and asks why anyone needed the extra elevation.

sources.institution: Victoria and Albert Museum via Google Arts & Culture
sources.locator: Pair of chopines; Venetian pair; 1600/1620; height 9 cm each; asset 8wFJYTRJPgEl_w
sources.verification_scope: Official source and stated anchors, not automatic semantic entailment

ideas.fact_boundary: The museum connects raised shoes and dress with status and identifies this indoor pair. The modern promotion system is fiction. Do not confuse these nine-centimetre shoes with other much taller examples, universalize the custom, invent a law, or make women the target of the joke.
research_questions: [VERIFICAR] Confirm the museum inventory number and distinguish direct physical evidence from curatorial interpretations of status before expanding the costume discussion.

ideas.title: Please Roll Before Joining the Meeting
ideas.era: Ur, Early Dynastic III; board dated circa 2600-2400 BCE
ideas.premise: What if today joining a team challenge required the right dice throw, using the entry rule described for the Royal Game of Ur?
ideas.benchmark_query: Please Roll Before Joining the Meeting history

rationale.curiosity: A simple participation hurdle reveals a specific surviving ancient board rather than claiming the oldest game.
rationale.cast_comedy: Pip can remain stuck outside while Rex confuses luck with merit; Mia can explain the actual rule boundary.
rationale.modern_contrast: Modern access screens become an explicitly fictional physical board-game queue.
rationale.primary_sources: British Museum identifies board 1928,1009.378 and separates surviving inlay from missing pieces; reconstructed rules require care.

cast_gags.crow: Raven opens the archive on a fictional login process involving dice.
cast_gags.pip: Pip prepares a perfect presentation but cannot enter the imagined team challenge.
cast_gags.mia: Mia stops Rex from treating a lucky roll as historical evidence of talent.
cast_gags.rex: Rex invents a leadership badge for reaching a rosette first.
cast_gags.timmy: Timmy reaches the waiting area with snacks while Pip is still rolling.

sources.institution: British Museum via Google Arts & Culture
sources.locator: The Royal Game of Ur; registration 1928,1009.378; Early Dynastic III; date field -2600/-2400
sources.verification_scope: Official source and stated anchors, not automatic semantic entailment

ideas.fact_boundary: The object and institutional description document a board and an entry condition described from ancient references. Modern workplace participation is fiction, not an ancient employment rule. Do not call Ur the origin of chess or backgammon; this board's own gaming pieces do not survive.
research_questions: [VERIFICAR] Identify the particular ancient rules document and its date before presenting one reconstruction as the exact rules used with this third-millennium board.

ideas.title: The Budget Speech That Added Three Zeros
ideas.era: United Kingdom, House of Commons, 8 April 1869
ideas.premise: What if today your finance meeting replayed an 1869 budget speech that inflated a hair-powder duty from 925 pounds to 925,000 before correcting itself?
ideas.benchmark_query: The Budget Speech That Added Three Zeros history

rationale.curiosity: A documented correction gives the hook a precise surprise without inventing a fiscal scandal.
rationale.cast_comedy: Rex can celebrate an imaginary windfall until Mia removes three zeros and Pip puts away the celebration.
rationale.modern_contrast: Spreadsheet scale errors provide an immediate modern analogy to a parliamentary speech.
rationale.primary_sources: Hansard supplies a dated primary speech with the mistaken and corrected figures; a proposed repeal is not proof of enactment.

cast_gags.crow: Raven distinguishes what a speaker said from what the Treasury actually collected.
cast_gags.pip: Pip orders imaginary celebration snacks before hearing the correction.
cast_gags.mia: Mia moves the decimal scale on Rex's fictional slide back into reality.
cast_gags.rex: Rex announces a vast budget increase and then quietly folds the slide into his pocket.
cast_gags.timmy: Timmy returns the giant celebration banner and keeps a tiny paper flag.

sources.locator: Ways and Means - Financial Statement; Commons 8 April 1869; hair-powder passage, columns 391-392
sources.verification_scope: Official source and stated anchors, not automatic semantic entailment

ideas.fact_boundary: The speech records a mistaken revenue figure and immediate correction while proposing abolition. The modern slide, celebration and actions are fiction. Do not claim the government actually collected the inflated amount or that this speech alone proves repeal, fraud, or modern purchasing power.
research_questions: [VERIFICAR] Check the enacted legislation before stating the repeal date; corroborate the corrected receipt with fiscal accounts if it becomes a substantive revenue claim.

ideas.title: Your Fridge Needs Another Delivery
ideas.era: United States, advertisement published 1913; earlier date field is separately qualified
ideas.premise: What if today your kitchen refrigerator needed replacement blocks of ice rather than just an electricity connection, as in the Monroe icebox advertisement?
ideas.benchmark_query: Your Fridge Needs Another Delivery history

rationale.curiosity: A familiar appliance with an unexpected consumable has an immediate, tangible reveal.
rationale.cast_comedy: Pip waits for a refill while Rex discovers that branding something modern does not eliminate maintenance.
rationale.modern_contrast: The routine electricity assumption turns into an explicitly fictional delivery-tracking problem.
rationale.primary_sources: Smithsonian locates a 1913 advertisement with a catalog ID; conflicting date fields and successful retrieval must be disclosed.

cast_gags.crow: Raven separates a real advertisement from claims about every historical household.
cast_gags.pip: Pip repeatedly refreshes an imaginary ice-delivery tracker before packing lunch.
cast_gags.mia: Mia checks the drip tray rather than accepting Rex's invented maintenance-free slogan.
cast_gags.rex: Rex attempts to sell a fictional app update for a cabinet that needs ice.
cast_gags.timmy: Timmy arrives with an empty lunch container and an inconveniently practical question.

sources.locator: The Monroe from American Homes and Gardens; catalog 182094; record silgoi_68369; publication 1913; separate Date field 1900-1905
sources.verification_scope: Official source and stated anchors, not automatic semantic entailment

ideas.fact_boundary: Institutional metadata identifies a magazine advertisement; its explanatory notes describe replacement ice and a drip tray. The publication date is not proof of manufacture date. The modern app and slogan are fiction; retrieval failures leave the source locally unverified, and no universal delivery interval or food-safety guarantee is asserted.
research_questions: [VERIFICAR] Read the original advertisement at a legible resolution, resolve the 1900-1905 versus 1913 metadata distinction, and document local supply conditions before quantifying ice use or cost.
